title: Nilakantha, the blue throat
hookLine: Nilakantha, the blue-throated: why Shiva drank the poison, and why devotees pour cool water over him
carry: shiva held the poison so the world wouldn't burn
tomorrow: why would anyone bow to God's anger?

cards: In paintings and posters of Shiva, look at his throat. It's blue. The throat carries a darker stain, like a bruise.
Some of his names describe how he looks or what he rules. This one remembers something he did, and marks the place on his body where it happened: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.

teach.b: Nila is blue, a dark blue-black, and kantha is the throat.

The story behind it is the churning of the ocean, told in the Mahabharata and the Puranas. The gods and the demons want amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it lies at the bottom of the ocean of milk.
So they make a churn out of a mountain, use the great serpent as the rope, and pull, the gods at one end and the demons at the other.
Treasures rise, and then something terrible: a poison, halahala, so strong it begins to burn the worlds. Nobody wants it. The gods and the demons both turn to Shiva.
And Shiva drinks it. In some tellings Parvati puts her hand to his throat so it won't go down; in others his own power holds it there. Either way, the poison stops at the throat and stains it blue.
So the name is a scar, worn openly. Here's the teaching Hindus act out with their hands. Shiva is the God who takes in what would destroy everyone else.
When they pour water or milk over the Shiva linga, the ritual bath called abhisheka, many families say it's to cool him, because the poison is still in his throat.
In the monsoon month of Shravan, which many say is when the churning happened, crowds of pilgrims carry river water for miles to pour over him.
Some teachers add a reading for family life: someone often holds the hard news so it doesn't spread, and the cool water is how you thank them.

how: Hindus tell the churning of the ocean in the Mahabharata and the Puranas; devotees honor Shiva as Nilakantha and pour water or milk over the Shiva linga in abhisheka, which many say cools the poison in his throat, especially in the month of Shravan.

a hymn of Shiva's names, here the blue throat that held poison
a story of how the demons poisoned Shiva in his sleep

s: Shiva's throat is blue because he was born that way
it's stained by the poison he drank at the churning of the ocean.
the poison was dangerous enough to burn the worlds
nobody wanted it, so the gods and demons both turned to Shiva.
every telling says the same thing stopped the poison
in some, Parvati's hand at his throat; in others, his own power.

games.q: a poison rises from the ocean and starts to burn the worlds. the gods and demons turn to you, Shiva. what do you do?
o: throw it back into the sea.
drink it, and hold it at your throat.
tell them to fix their own mess.
games.why: Shiva drinks the halahala. it stops at his throat and stains it blue, so he's called Nilakantha.

practice: If you can, hold a glass of water. Breathe slowly through the throat, cool on the way in, warm on the way out.
Let one hard thing from this week come to mind, a sharp word you heard or nearly said, and let it rest at the throat for a breath or two, not pushed down and not thrown back.
Then take a slow sip, the way devotees pour cool water for Nilakantha. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya softly; if you don't, just notice the cool.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Nilakantha, the blue-throated, who drank the poison from the churning ocean and held it at his throat.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Nilakantha, blue (nila) throat (kantha); Shiva after drinking the poison.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva held the poison so the world wouldn't burn. That's why the cool water is poured. Go gently.
